sections.title: Warm-up
sections.prompt: Read the pairs aloud. Say the pronoun and the verb as one unit, without a pause.
items: Ich bin müde. Ich habe Hunger.
sections.lede: sein and haben are short words, so practise them as rhythm, not as grammar.

sections.title: Learning objectives
sections.lede: By the end of this lesson you will be able to describe yourself and say what you have.

sections.title: The big picture
sections.lede: Two irregular verbs carry a huge share of everyday German: sein (to be) and haben (to have).

blocks.text: sein and haben are the most useful verbs in the language, and both are irregular. That means you cannot build them from a pattern; you learn six forms and then use them constantly. In the present tense they need no helper verb: Ich bin müde is simply “I am tired”, not “I do be tired”.
Ich bin Lehrerin und habe zwei Kinder.
blocks.en: I am a teacher and have two children.

items: Use sein for identity and origin: Ich bin Anna. Wir sind aus Chile.
Use sein for states and descriptions: Er ist müde. Das Zimmer ist klein.
Use haben for possession: Ich habe ein Fahrrad. Sie hat einen Hund.
Age uses sein, not haben: Ich bin dreißig Jahre alt. The word alt is required.

blocks.title: No article with professions
blocks.text: In German you say Ich bin Lehrer, not Ich bin ein Lehrer. The same applies to nationalities and religions: Sie ist Ärztin. Er ist Spanier.

sections.title: Rules & patterns
sections.lede: Learn the two tables as whole blocks. They are worth the effort.

items: The ich form of sein is bin, not “be”. The du form is bist.
ihr seid is the only form with -d. Do not say “ihr sind”.
wir, sie and Sie share the same forms: sind and haben.
haben is regular in the plural but irregular in the singular: habe, hast, hat.

blocks.title: Why einen?
blocks.text: The thing you have is the direct object, so it takes the accusative. Only masculine changes: der becomes den, and ein becomes einen. Feminine and neuter stay the same.

sections.title: Vocabulary
sections.lede: Two verbs and four nouns give you a complete family description.

items.example: Mein Bruder ist zwölf Jahre alt.
items.exampleEn: My brother is twelve years old.

sections.title: Example sentences
sections.lede: Notice how often sein describes something and haben shows possession.

items.en: I am a teacher by profession.

items.note: die Türkei is feminine, so aus takes the dative der.

items.de: Ich habe einen Bruder und eine Schwester.
items.en: I have a brother and a sister.
items.note: Bruder is masculine, so ein becomes einen; Schwester is feminine and stays eine.
Eltern is plural, so the verb is haben.

sections.title: Pronunciation
sections.lede: These forms are short. Clear vowels matter more than speed.

items.hint: A short i, as in English “tin”: bin. Do not stretch it into “bean”.
Short i, then a crisp st: bist. The s is sharp.
A long, voiced s like English z, then a long i: zeyt. It sounds exactly like seit (“since”), so context decides the meaning.
HAH-buh. Long a, and the final e is a weak “uh”.
BROO-der. Long u; the final -er is soft, not a strong English “er”.

blocks.text: Hast du Geschwister? (“Do you have siblings?”) is a normal question among new acquaintances, and so is Woher kommst du? A question about age is also common, but it is more direct than in English: Wie alt bist du? is fine among friends, while Wie alt sind Sie? is safer in formal situations.

When Germans give their age, the word alt is required: Ich bin dreißig Jahre alt. In fast speech you may hear Ich bin dreißig, but a written sentence should keep Jahre alt. Notice that German uses sein here, not haben.

sections.title: Dialogue in context
sections.lede: Two classmates compare their families. Listen for bin, bist, ist and hat.

lines.speaker: Lena
lines.en: Hello Tim! Do you have siblings?

lines.speaker: Tim
lines.de: Ja, ich habe eine Schwester. Sie ist sechzehn.
lines.en: Yes, I have a sister. She is sixteen.

lines.speaker: Lena
lines.de: Und du? Bist du auch sechzehn?
lines.en: And you? Are you sixteen too?

lines.speaker: Tim
lines.de: Nein, ich bin achtzehn. Und du?
lines.en: No, I am eighteen. And you?

lines.speaker: Lena
lines.de: Ich habe einen Bruder. Er ist zwölf.
lines.en: I have a brother. He is twelve.

lines.speaker: Tim
lines.de: Meine Schwester hat auch einen Hund. Er heißt Max.
lines.en: My sister also has a dog. His name is Max.

sections.title: Grammar spotlight
sections.heading: sein and haben side by side
sections.lede: Compare the two verbs form by form, then add the accusative for haben.

items: A statement starts with the subject and puts the verb second: Ich bin müde. Du hast Zeit.
A yes/no question puts the verb first: Bist du müde? Hast du Zeit?
Negate with nicht after the verb: Ich bin nicht müde. Ich habe keine Zeit.
With haben, the object is in the accusative: einen Bruder, eine Schwester, ein Auto.

sections.tip: When you learn a new noun, learn its article too. That article decides whether haben needs einen, eine or ein.

sections.title: Choose the right answer
sections.lede: Pick the form that agrees with the pronoun.

exercises.explanation: The ich form of sein is bin: Ich bin aus Portugal.
du takes hast: Hast du Geschwister?
wir takes sind: Wir sind Lehrer.
er takes hat: Er hat einen Hund.
ihr takes seid: Ihr seid sehr freundlich.
der Bruder is masculine, so the accusative of ein is einen. Possession uses haben, not sein.

sections.title: Complete the sentence
sections.lede: Type the correct form of sein or haben.

exercises.explanation: Age uses sein: Ich bin 25 Jahre alt.
The du form of haben is hast.
wir, sie and Sie all take sind. Here Sie means “they” or polite “you”.
er/sie/es takes ist. Mein Bruder = he.
wir takes haben: Wir haben ein Haus.
The yes/no question puts the verb first: Seid ihr müde?

sections.title: Build the sentence
sections.lede: Keep the verb in second position in statements.

exercises.explanation: haben comes second, and the masculine object takes einen.
sein comes second, then the origin with aus.

exercises.prompt: Build: “My sister is ten years old.”
exercises.answer: Meine Schwester ist zehn Jahre alt.

exercises.explanation: A yes/no question starts with the verb, and Hund is masculine: einen Hund.

sections.title: Speaking
sections.lede: Describe yourself and one family member in four short sentences.
sections.prompt: Say your name, your age, and what you have. Then describe one family member with sein.

model.de: Ich bin Mia. Ich bin zweiundzwanzig Jahre alt. Ich habe einen Bruder. Er ist Student.
model.en: I am Mia. I am twenty-two years old. I have a brother. He is a student.

tips: Use sein for who you are and how old you are; use haben only for things you possess.
Check the article of the noun before you choose einen, eine or ein.
Say the four sentences twice: the second time without looking at the model.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.lede: Most errors with these two verbs come from English word order or a missing word.

items.why: German needs alt after the number of years: Ich bin 20 Jahre alt.
The ihr form of sein is seid, not sind. Sind belongs to wir, sie and Sie.
Bruder is masculine. In the accusative, ein becomes einen.
Schwester is feminine, so the article is eine in both nominative and accusative.

sections.lede: Eight questions. Score 70% or more to unlock the next lesson.

questions.explanation: The ich form of sein is bin.
du takes hast: Hast du einen Bruder?
sie (she) takes hat, and Schwester is feminine: eine Schwester.
wir sind = we are; müde = tired.
The ihr form of sein is seid.
The ich form of haben is habe.
Age uses sein + Jahre alt, with the verb in second position.
Yes/no questions start with the verb. Auto is neuter, so ein stays ein.
